To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. ## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

I’ll read the last two reviews and the broad-base win in game 30, then play White against 20k. I’ll track connections, eye-making turns, and area, and save the full game and lessons for the next session.

## Two left corners did not ensure a broad living framework

C3/C7 took both left corners; E7/E5 broadened toward the upper center.
White D2/C2 undercut the bottom, while D4/D5/C5 formed a wedge between the two Black bases.
D3 directly joined C3, and C4 kept that chain moving leftward.
E6 joined E5/E7, but White C5 at14 prevented a direct C4–C5–C6–C7 connection.
D6 capped the wedge and joined E6; White E3 then left the lower C3/C4/D3 only B3/B4.
B4/B5/B6/B7 required four turns to carry that chain around the wedge and join C7.
These were useful actual connected moves, but they did not add enough territory to replace the lost lower boundary.

D7 was available for a direct upper/left join and was eventually played at39.
Before D7, C7 and D6/E7 were not connected across their shared empty point.
The broad left outline was still conditional, and its joins competed with expansion turns.
No earlier C5, D7, different opening or individual move value is established as a winning replacement.
A two-corner opening still needs a concrete connection and eye schedule before central cuts force a long detour.

At move25 the explicit selected left27 was:
A/B/C rows4–9=18, excluding White C5/C6 gives16;
C3/D3 gives2;
D6/D7/E5/E6/E7 gives5;
D8/D9/E8/E9 gives4.
Total27. Several endpoints were unplayed and no secure27 claim was made.
G/H/J rows1–5=15 would give42, below Black45 even if both outlines lived.
This prompted a second-base attempt, but its life plan was inadequate.

## Separate the successful upper-right expansion from the failed lower foothold

G3 at25 entered the open lower-right with G2/H3 liberties after White G4.

H2 supplied H1/J2/J3, but did not produce two eyes.
White F1 also narrowed the bottom boundary.
At this stage a claimed nine-point corner was a contested outline, not owned area or life.
A wider second base with actual connections was needed; the fact that the corner was initially open did not prove an eye schedule.

J3 at43 joined G3/H2/H3 and reduced White's central eleven stones from three liberties to E2/F2.

The inventory was exact before play. The error was choosing a move without a viable survival plan, rather than a missed liberty.

I stopped adding lower stones. White J2 at64 captured the four.

White E2 would capture that attacking stone and connect its own groups.
Black E2 would start E1/F2, and White F2 would connect central/F1/G2 while atariing it atE1.

If White E8 were played, it would have soleF8; Black F8 joins F7/G8 and captures E8, while E9 still retains F9.

H8 at63 joined H9/J8 to G8/main.

The main also has true F6, J6, J9 and separate G7/H7 two-point eye space.

## Area accounting

At Black35 the explicit upper conditional45 was:
A/B rows5–9=10;
C7/C8/C9=3;
D6/D7/D8/D9=4;
E/F/G/H/J rows5–9=25, excluding White G7 gives24;

A sufficient sum did not guarantee the lower life, upper containment or left endpoints.

Upper45 lost A5/A6/A7 (3).
White B8/C8/C9/D9 and their A8/A9/B9 room removed seven more.
Capturing G7 restored one point initially excluded from that outline; H7/H8 were already included.
45−3−7+1=36.
The whole lower target failed and cannot remain in the score.
F8/E9 retained coordinates already inside the selected outline; H8 divided life room and did not expand it.

Final Black28 stones+8 territory=36:
E8 (1), F6 (1), F9/G9 (2), G7/H7 (2), J6 (1), J9 (1).
White29+16=45:
A1/A2/B1/C1/D1/E1 (6);
A8/A9/B9 (3);
F2 (1), G1 (1), G3/H2/H3/J3 (4), J1 (1).
No dead or neutral points; 45+7−36=16 matches the official score.
Black rows1–9:0,0,2,2,6,7,8,6,5.

These specified replies prevent that local sacrifice from forcing a capture; no exhaustive attack claim.

2. Corners plus unplayed shared connection points do not form a connected framework. White D4/D5/C5 forced a four-turn B4/B5/B6/B7 detour.
3. The useful second-base development was connected H5/G5/F5/J5; the separate G3/H3 lower foothold never had a verified two-eye schedule.
4. G2 and H1 are concrete lower life deadlines. After J3/H1 the four Black stones had soleJ2; J2/J1 would lose five. Accurate inventories must change move choice.
5. Two enemy liberties are not atari. A one-liberty Black F2 attack could be captured by E2; avoid rescues based on ignored capture.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
